summary: Investigates security threats and risks for Open Pluggable Edge Services and how those threats affect the underlying architecture. It is for discovering and analyzing threats and does not specify or recommend solutions.

plainLanguage.summary: OPES processors and remote callout servers can analyze and transform messages between a data provider and consumer. RFC 3837 catalogs the security and privacy risks this creates but does not propose solutions.

questions: risks of open pluggable edge services
what are the security threats of opes
why does opes break end to end encryption
subtitle: Risks created when processors can inspect and transform application messages in transit.

tldr.problem: Open Pluggable Edge Services (OPES) processors and callout servers can inspect or change application messages, creating risks for providers and consumers.
tldr.mechanism: The memo analyzes threats to the data flow and to separate control information, from both insiders and outsiders.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3837 is a threat analysis only. It does not specify or recommend solutions, and its scope is threats introduced by OPES processors and callout servers.

facts.label: Threat categories analyzed
facts.value: Data-flow threats and out-of-band control-data threats

today: RFC 3837 is an Informational memo published in August 2004. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; the memo is a threat analysis and defines no protocol.

sections.title: OPES Components and Scope
sections.content:
Open Pluggable Edge Services (OPES) allow application services to operate between a data provider and a data consumer. An OPES processor may analyze or transform application messages and may use remote callout servers to perform some work.

The memo considers effects on both provider and consumer applications, and distinguishes insiders that participate in the OPES system from outsiders. Insiders can cause harm intentionally or through configuration errors, faulty software or compromised networks. The document discovers and analyzes threats; it does not recommend solutions.
sections.plainLanguage: OPES processors and callout servers can read or change application messages in transit. The memo studies risks to both the sender's and receiver's applications without proposing fixes.

sections.title: Risks in the Data Flow
sections.content:
An OPES processor is placed where it can intercept application traffic and run code that analyzes or modifies that traffic. The memo notes that this creates conditions for a man-in-the-middle attack. A compromised processor or callout server may affect every provider using the service.

Common application protocols may provide weak privacy, authentication and integrity. The architecture's requirement not to disrupt clients and servers that do not know about OPES also means those clients may not use safeguards introduced through protocol extensions.
sections.plainLanguage: A processor can see and modify passing application data, so compromising it can affect multiple services. Clients that do not support OPES extensions may not be able to use added safeguards.

sections.title: Network-Level Attacks
sections.content:
Processors and callout servers can face attacks from outsiders and from networks belonging to other service providers. The memo identifies IP spoofing, session stealing, snooping, sabotage, theft of service and denial of service as network-level risks.

Spurious requests can consume CPU, memory and network-interface capacity. An attacker may also coordinate many nodes to send requests at once. A faulty implementation that interferes with end-to-end addressing or flow control could contribute to wider network congestion.
sections.plainLanguage: Attackers can target the processor or callout server directly, including by sending enough false requests to consume its resources. Network-level weaknesses may also affect routing or flow control.

sections.title: Application-Level Threats
sections.content:
The memo lists threats from unauthorized OPES entities and actions, unwanted transformations, corrupted content and changes to message structure. An authorized service may still perform a transformation that one party did not expect, or a compromised server may inject false information.

Fine-grained permissions are difficult to express and verify. Changing headers or transforming related data inconsistently can break end-to-end integrity, references or the meaning of content. The memo suggests that a fine-grained policy language could be developed, possibly enforced with digital signatures, but does not define one.
sections.plainLanguage: A processor may perform an action beyond the permission it received, alter content unexpectedly or deliver corrupted data. The memo says it can be difficult to define and check exactly which parts of a message may change.

sections.title: Encryption, Integrity and Tracing
sections.content:
OPES services generally cannot transform data protected by end-to-end encryption unless processors receive decryption keys, which would compromise the intended confidentiality. Services that modify data also conflict with end-to-end integrity protection. Defining replacement hop-by-hop protections is outside the memo's scope.

Tracing and notification facilities may be vulnerable or lack standards. Weak authentication between processors and callout servers can expose the flow to denial of service and other attacks. The memo also notes that failure of the OPES system may prevent a consumer application from accessing data.
sections.plainLanguage: Processors cannot read end-to-end encrypted data without access to the keys. Changing data also conflicts with end-to-end integrity checks, and tracing or notification systems can have their own weaknesses.

sections.title: Risks in Control Information
sections.content:
OPES separates application data from control information such as rulesets, trust setup, tracing and policy updates. The architecture sets requirements but prescribes no mechanism, leaving implementations responsible for protecting data, authenticating entities and authorizing actions.

Threats include inaccurate accounting that can cause incorrect charges or payments, denial of service requests, inconsistent privacy policy, exposure of privacy preferences or security settings, and improper policy enforcement. A misconfiguration can also cause the processor to ignore a consumer application.
sections.plainLanguage: Separate control information includes rules, accounting and privacy settings. If it is changed, exposed or enforced incorrectly, users may be charged wrongly or lose expected protections.
